1uouK7mzsxuY1Xx9F4_ZjfG_Bv5--HSbX.note: Hampi, the city of ruins, where every stone seems to hold a story. I visited in early 2019 with a newly bought mirrorless camera, and its ancient character felt perfect for experimenting with black and white. The monochrome frames brought out a sense of longing, age, and the forgotten grandeur of the Vijayanagara Empire. Seeing the ruins today, I could only imagine how magnificent this city must have been in its full glory. And by the banks of the Tungabhadra, the Virupaksha Temple still stands: timeless, silent, and unforgettable.

17sFhhUTnrPpNa8QL90tlkk3aeRfw4_M4.title: New York
17sFhhUTnrPpNa8QL90tlkk3aeRfw4_M4.note: My city of dreams. Six visits in, New York still feels new. Between subway chaos, restless streets and the lights of Times Square, I keep finding moments of calm and more reasons to fall in love.

experience.title: The city that still surprises me
experience.subtitle: New York City · July 2023
paragraphs: In July 2023, my friends and I planned a trip to New York almost on impulse. We were students, and finding a place to stay in the middle of summer was not easy. But we had seen this city so many times in movies that I wanted to feel its energy for myself. We boarded a bus in Boston and headed for the city that never sleeps.

Just before the bus entered the Holland Tunnel, the skyline opened up in front of us. I can still remember looking out at it from the road and feeling my heart skip a beat. It was the beginning of one of the best trips I have ever taken with friends.

We did the iconic Shah Rukh Khan pose on the Brooklyn Bridge and wandered through Bethesda Terrace in Central Park. We stood in line at Adele's for three hours, only to decide that, for us, the food was just average. None of it spoiled the fun. Sweating through the summer heat, we wanted to see everything: Magnolia Bakery, the train from Jersey City, Broadway glowing at night, and the Oculus.

The highlight was sunset at SUMMIT One Vanderbilt. Even the elevator ride felt like we were entering a larger world. Then we were above the skyline, with the Empire State Building and the Chrysler Building in view, watching the city change in the evening light. For a while, all I wanted to do was stand there and take it in.

Grand Central Terminal stayed with me too. I loved its vintage architecture and the little details, even the shoe-shine stands. I had known it from the final dance scene in Friends with Benefits, but being there felt different. People moved through it in every direction, and somehow it still felt like one central gathering place: the heartbeat of the city, with the streets and trains flowing out from it like veins.

I could keep talking about New York forever. I have visited six times, and I still do not tire of it. After my hometown, it is the only city I can imagine living in. To me, it really is the best city in the world.

1BoLvYoSCyQSDrGcBt7Ey1g4b_8Ud5Uiv.note: On my first visit to Bhutan, its quiet streets, mountain landscapes and peaceful monasteries stayed with me. I photographed the journey on a newly bought OnePlus 7 Pro.

experience.title: My first glimpse of Bhutan
experience.subtitle: Paro, Thimphu and Punakha · photographed on a OnePlus 7 Pro
paragraphs: Bhutan shares a border with India and is only a few hours by air from Kolkata, yet I felt I had arrived somewhere entirely different. I noticed it as soon as I landed: in the way people spoke, in the traditional clothes I saw around me, and in the pride they took in their culture.

The streets felt unusually quiet. I hardly heard a horn, and our guides were careful about littering or disturbing the places we visited. Learning that Bhutan is carbon-negative made that care for its surroundings feel even more remarkable. Mobile data felt expensive there too, another detail I still remember from the trip.

The landscape seemed to change around every bend. In Paro, Thimphu and Punakha, the towns, valleys and Himalayan mountains were beautiful in different ways. Tiger's Nest is the place everyone talks about, but I found just as much beauty in the quieter stops along the road.

The shrines and monasteries stayed with me most. I could sit inside one and lose track of time. There was a stillness that made me want to slow down, listen and simply be there. The kindness of the people I met and the local food made those days feel even warmer.

I had recently bought a OnePlus 7 Pro, the company's flagship phone at the time, and I made every photograph and video from this trip with it. I wanted to hold on to the mountain views, the streets and the peaceful moments inside the monasteries. Looking at these pictures now brings me back to the wonder of seeing Bhutan for the first time.

178EBXiTz-Qjls1p99Ax8HliYeJTRpBwT.note: Ranganathittu has been part of my journey from a frightened eight-year-old in a boat to a photographer finding peace in the patience of watching birds. These photographs bring together what I have learnt along the way.

experience.title: Learning to be still
experience.subtitle: A childhood fear, my first camera, and the patience birds taught me.
paragraphs: I first visited Ranganathittu when I was around eight, during a trip to Mysuru. To that little boy, the place felt almost frightening. There were these enormous birds flying overhead, calling and screaming all around us. Everything seemed louder and bigger than I was prepared for.

And then there were the crocodiles. We children had heard stories about them taking people who put their hands into the river during a boat ride. Those were the stories in my head as we stepped into the boat. I spent the entire ride sitting between my mother and my elder sister, watching the water and staying close to them.

When I returned in my twelfth grade, I had my first camera. It was a small one, and I knew very little about editing, lighting or photographic technique. What I did have was the hope that I could make something of myself in photography. I wanted to see what I could capture.

By a later visit, I had upgraded my camera and had a 200–600mm lens. I had learnt a little about technique, about building a composition, and about being patient enough to wait for it. I could sit freely in the boat now. The crocodiles in the water no longer filled me with the fear I remembered from childhood.

A naturalist at the sanctuary suggested a two-hour boat ride instead of the usual thirty minutes. My parents were deeply enthusiastic about nature themselves, and about giving their son the chance to make photographs he would remember for a lifetime. We took the longer ride. It became one of my most memorable experiences with a camera.

I photographed anything and everything that caught my eye. I kept reviewing my compositions, trying again, and waiting for the moment I had pictured. I watched a painted stork, waiting for it to take flight and return to the branch where it was feeding its young. I waited for birds to hunt, to drink from the river, and for the little movements that could change a frame. There were crocodiles sunbathing, too. For those two hours, I had the time of my life. I came away with the photographs I had imagined and planned for.

Bird photography taught me how quickly a moment can escape. With a larger animal, I could often follow its movement through the lens. These flying machines could bank and change direction in a second. Just when I thought I had followed one, it would be somewhere else. Tracking them asked something different of me.

Somehow, that challenge gave me an enormous sense of peace. I learnt to be quiet, to watch, and to wait. A single sound could be enough to lose the moment. So I would sit in that stillness and wait, and wait again, until the picture I was hoping for came together.

This collection is a commemoration of my journey in bird photography so far. It holds the memory of that frightened child in the boat, the student with his first small camera, and the time my parents gave me to stay on the river and keep photographing.

I have come to believe that a photographer who learns to follow birds can bring that skill to photographing mammals, while experience with larger animals alone does not prepare you for birds. That is my experience of the challenge. Nature puts you through its own training, and patience is something you have to earn.

experience.title: My first forest
experience.subtitle: Kanha, 2004. An evening in the forest, a photograph by my father, and the beginning of my love for wildlife.
paragraphs: I was seven when I first visited Kanha National Park in 2004. It was early March, spring in North India, and the evening air was turning chilly. Film cameras were what we had access to then. I did not know that one evening in the forest would stay with me for so long.

I still remember the gypsies parked beside a dried-up lake bed. On one side of the road, the ground sloped down towards the lake bed; on the other, tall grass stretched across the meadow. Someone in one of the gypsies had spotted a tiger in the bushes. Our driver was sure it might cross the road and go down towards the lake bed, so we waited with everyone else.

We stayed there for around half an hour. The sun was setting at the edge of my vision when a naturalist in the first jeep noticed movement in the bushes along the meadow. Within five minutes, the tiger appeared: a young male, perhaps three or four years old. The naturalist told us he had recently separated from his mother.

He came within about ten feet of me. Around fifteen jeeps had gathered, with people taking pictures and gasping at the sight. In all that chaos, I had only one real glance. But I remember the almost royal confidence in the way he moved. He crossed the road without hesitation, as though none of us were there.
That was the moment I fell in love with wildlife. The thrill of seeing a tiger so close was immense, and so was the respect I felt for the animal and its natural habitat.

After the trip, we waited for the film to be developed at the shop. When the photographs came back, I could hardly believe what my dad had captured: the tiger leaping from the gravel into the lake bed. He had made that picture with a film camera, with no display to check and no second take. It happened in an instant, and he caught it. Seeing those photographs made me want to find moments like that through my own camera.

My fondness for wildlife and my respect for the places it lives have only grown since that day. This collection is a small personal tribute to the 17 national parks I have visited over the years, and to the journey that began in Kanha.

1nSNRJDPWxHDbFxKBsxuNKD8Jg-PJEaSk.title: Washington
1nSNRJDPWxHDbFxKBsxuNKD8Jg-PJEaSk.note: Washington, DC leaves me in awe at every turn. Beyond its power, I love the marble halls, intricate carvings and quiet of its reading rooms. From the reflecting pool to spring blossoms, there is beauty in every direction.
